A_target.statement:
Let $H$ be a [[Definition:Hilbert Space|Hilbert space]].
Then every [[Definition:Non-Empty Set|non-empty]] [[Definition:Closed Set (Metric Space)|closed]] [[Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)|convex]] set $C \subseteq H$ has a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] nearest point to each $x \in H$, and for every closed subspace $M$:
:$H = M \oplus M^\perp$

B_source.statement: In $\R^n$ with the [[Definition:Dot Product|dot product]], every subspace $M$ satisfies $\R^n = M \oplus M^\perp$, and every vector has an expansion in an [[Definition:Orthonormal Basis|orthonormal basis]].

substitutions.the finite-dimensional space: a possibly infinite-dimensional space with an inner product
substitutions.the finite orthonormal basis: a countable orthonormal system with convergent expansions

derived.the orthogonal projection onto a subspac: the projection onto a closed subspace
derived.the finite expansion in a basis: a convergent series, with Bessel's inequality controlling the coefficients

object_map.reformulation: Drop the finiteness of dimension and replace compactness arguments by completeness ones.

validity_conditions: Euclidean space is the finite-dimensional case, so the generalization is faithful and every statement specializes correctly.
Completeness replaces compactness: the nearest point is obtained from a minimizing sequence shown to be Cauchy via the parallelogram law, not from compactness of a closed ball.

Closedness of the subspace is essential in infinite dimensions, since a non-closed subspace has no orthogonal complement decomposition; in finite dimensions every subspace is closed and the hypothesis is invisible.
proof_plan: Replace $\R^n$ by a [[Definition:Complete Metric Space|complete]] [[Definition:Inner Product Space|inner product space]] of arbitrary dimension.

Let $d = \displaystyle \inf_{y \mathop \in C} 
orm {x - y}$ and choose $y_n \in C$ with $
orm {x - y_n} 	o d$.
By the [[Parallelogram Law (Inner Product Space)|parallelogram law]] and convexity:
:$
orm {y_n - y_m}^2 \le 2 
orm {x - y_n}^2 + 2 
orm {x - y_m}^2 - 4 d^2 	o 0$
So $\sequence {y_n}$ is [[Definition:Cauchy Sequence (Metric Space)|Cauchy]], and converges in $C$ to the nearest point.

For a closed subspace $M$, let $P x$ be the nearest point in $M$.
Then $x - P x \perp M$, giving:
:$x = P x + \paren {x - P x} \in M \oplus M^\perp$
